errors.location: drafted.readdown.ann_115.evidence[2]; drafted.blocks[0]; drafted.worth_checking[0] (C059, C061, C003, C004)
errors.statement: Very little schooling lowers the predicted chance of a low income: 1st-4th grade about 10%, 7th-8th grade about 19% (worth_checking: the model gives people whose highest education is 1st-4th / 7th-8th grade a much lower chance than high-school graduates)
errors.check: probe --hold typical --sweep education=11,3,5 --sweep education-num=2,4,9,10: 9.9% / 19.3% only with education-num held at 10 (no 1st-4th grader has a level other than 2). With matching levels 1st-4th (level 2) 89.8%, 7th-8th (level 4) 86.5% vs high-school graduate (level 9) 73.8%. subgroup education=='3': n=189, typical-case risk 95.8%. The direction is reversed for every real person in the named group; the claims' own data test says 'disagrees'. The same wrong numbers appear in three places of the draft and are grouped here (both verifiers graded the worth_checking copy weakened only because it is flagged; it still states the artefact as what the model gives these people).

errors.statement: Typical person (a high-school graduate ...) predicted about 62%
errors.check: probe: high-school category at education-num 10 gives 61.9% (reproduces); at level 9 (every real high-school graduate) 73.8%. Right for the reference case the sentence defines, but that case is off-support.

errors.statement: A wife gets about 27% against a husband's 62%
errors.check: probe --sweep relationship=0,5 --sweep sex=1,0: wife+male 27.1% (3 training rows), wife+female 47.4%, husband+male 61.9%. Direction right; the size comes from an off-support male-wife case.

probe --sweep marital-status=2,4 --sweep relationship=0,1: never married but still a husband 87.5% (reproduces, off-support); with a consistent role (not in a family) married 83.6%, never married 95.6%. Direction right, size understated.

errors.statement: Women get a higher predicted chance than men: about 80% against 62%
errors.check: probe relationship x sex: 79.7% is a female husband (1 row). The sex term is +0.88 log-odds at every fixed role, so the sentence is right with role held fixed, but a typical married woman (wife, 47.4%) is below a typical married man (61.9%).

errors.statement: A doctorate makes no difference for people born in Cambodia (n = 19)
errors.check: probe --set native-country=1 --sweep education=11,10 --sweep education-num=9,16: at a fixed education level the doctorate category changes nothing in the whole model (65.6% = 65.6%, 3.9% = 3.9%), so the statement holds model-wide, not only through the part as B says. It fails only if 'a doctorate' includes the jump in education-num to 16 (65.6% to 3.9%), a reading that would change every doctorate sentence in the draft. subgroup education_10==1 and native-country_1==1: n = 0, so no real counterexample exists. A scope/wording issue (worth flagging that the level effect dominates), not refuted. Verifier A upheld this sentence.

errors.statement: Capital gains lower the predicted chance slowly at first, then faster: about 62% at 0 to about 6% at 6849 US dollars
errors.check: probe --sweep capital-gain=0,2500,5000,6849: 61.9%, 39.1%, 20.2%, 6.4%. On the chance scale the fall is fastest first (22.8 then 18.9 points per 2500 dollars, then 13.8 over 1849); 'slowly then faster' holds only on the log-odds scale (slope steepens past the hinge at about 5250 dollars; ann_117 is -0.63 at 6849). The end points reproduce.

errors.statement: People under 35 ... adding 0.98 to the log-odds on average for the 16,819 training rows it acts on
errors.check: subgroup age >= 35: n = 22254, ann_116 acts on 100% of them with contribution -0.4263; the under-35 rows get +0.9789. The 0.98 and 16,819 reproduce, but the part acts on every row (always-on unit), so 'rows it acts on' is the wrong scope; relative to the older group the young gain about 1.41. The technical hypothesis states it correctly.
